content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a few-shot learning methods for graph data, in particular addressing the problems of node classification and graph classification. 
The proposed method consists of three steps
1) a contrastive self-supervised learning method similar to BYOL (Grill et al, 2020).
2) a distillation stage where the student learns from the teacher obtained in step (i), teacher and student see different augmentations of the same input. 
3) a few-shot learning stage based on MAML (Finn et al, 2017).

Experiments consider 5 datasets and 14 baseline models for node classification.
For graph classification 4 datasets are used and 11 baseline models.  
Experiments show consistent improvements of the proposed method over existing baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths

* Experiments are conducted along two problems (graph and node classification), and include multiple datasets for each, and results are compared to a wide range of baseline models. 

* The proposed method consistently improves over the baseline approaches. 

# Weaknesses  

* Different baseline models are used for graph and node classification experiments, it is not clear why the same set of baselines can't be used for both. 

* Experiments do not explicitly state that results for baseline methods were obtained by the authors. I'm assuming this is the case, as the authors refer to the codebases for the baseline methods in the supplementary material. There is no comparison of results obtained by the authors to results reported in the original papers. 

* Some ablations are missing: 
what happens if you only apply the MAML-based third stage of the approach?  
What happens if you apply the SSL and distillation stage, but replace the MAML-based stage with another approach, eg kNN?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity
* The paper is well written and generally easy to follow. 
That being said, some specific points were unclear

* in section 4.1 on page 4, it is explained that both branches of the SSL graph learning model use a different head: using 1 vs 2 MLP layers, which is motivated by ensuring both branches do not give rise to exactly the same features, and thus avoid representation collapse. Yet the loss in eq (3) drives both branches to yield the same output. This seems to go against the design choice of using 1 vs 2 MLP layers. An ablation of the effect of using the same nr of layers in both branches would be useful to understand the impact of this design choice. 
* Section 4.3 presents an approximation of conditional entropy of the input graph given the latent graph embedding. The presentation is unclear in several places. 
Equation 13 seems not to hold, and notation is unclear: does the integration go over all latent node embeddings? Can the authors provide a proof of the equality, as it seems non-trivial or erroneous.
The notation z=f(x) on the first line of page 6 seem incorrect, as the latent embedding of one node also depends on the other nodes in the input graph. 
In general, in this section it is not clear what material is taken from Ma et al, 2019, and which part of the material is new. 
* There is no definition of the "feature masking" data augmentation. 
* The definition of k-shot setting was not clear for the experiments: does it mean k fully annotated graphs are given for both node and graph classification settings? Or do we have k labeled nodes in a single graph for node classification?
* Similarly, it is not clear how the "label rate" is defines, and how it interacts with the shot number. 


# Quality
* The experimental evaluation is thorough: two classification problems are considered (node classification and graph classification), both are evaluated on a number of datasets, and compared to a large collection of existing methods. 
* Ablations evaluate the different data augmentations that are used, and validates their complementarity. 
* Most experiments consider the 3 and 5-shot setting, for a selection of datasets and baselines, graphs analyse the classification accuracy as a function of the shot-number and the labelling rate. 


# Novelty
The paper presents a few-shot learning technique for graph data, which is moderately novel.
The novelty resides in the combination of several existing ideas (BYOL, distillation, MAML), and chaining them together in the context of graph neural networks. 

# Reproducibility 
The experiments seem reproducible with some effort. 
Authors provide code to reproduce results obtained with their method. 
Released code does not seem to allow to reproduce results for all reported baselines. 
Links to the code for other baselines are provided in the supplementary material.
For the datasets used references to the corresponding papers are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper presents a novel few-shot graph neural network approach. 
It integrates SSL pre-training, and self-distillation steps, and a MAML-like few-shot learning stage. 
Extensive experimental results show improvements over existing methods, and some ablations are provided. 
Overall the paper is well written, but some parts require more details (experimental setup) and some technical details are unclear (mutual information estimation). 
The experimental results are quite convincing (but it seems no results from other papers on the same datasets are reported), on the other hand the method is not very original but consists in a relatively straightforward combination of existing ideas.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper explores the effect of graph contrastive learning in the graph few-shot learning (GFL) problem.   

Specifically, the training is divided into three phases: (1) regular graph contrastive learning, (2) contrastive knowledge distillation, and (3) graph meta-learning.   
Typical contrastive and graph contrastive learning designs are used in this paper, e.g., moving average updates, stop-gradient, asymmetric design, and feature normalization.   

In addition, the authors proposed a quantitative measurement method based on conditional entropy between the feature embeddings and original information. 

As to the experiment, various GFS and Graph learning baselines are compared. Analysis of the shot number, augmentation, and loss info is conducted.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
- This paper verifies again the effectiveness of contrastive learning in graph representation, especially in the few labeled setting. 
- The overall structure is simple but is overall reasonable. 
- The proposed quantitative measure is an effective indicator according to the experiments. 
- Experiments are conducted on two tasks w.r.t various datasets and baseline methods. 

# Weaknesses
- Since the effectiveness of contrastive learning has already been investigated in various graph learning settings, the contribution of applying existing graph contrastive learning techniques in the GFL setting is limited and kind of incremental. 
- The teacher-student design improved the basic contrastive graph learning performance, but this knowledge and design are also common in the context of graph learning, few-shot learning, and contrastive learning. 
- In this case, this paper seems to be a combination of existing working techniques in the graph few-shot learning setting. 
- In Figure 1, the online GNN and target GNN do not have feature normalization; why is this different from the teacher-student branch? Is this a typo? If not, Eq. (3) is incorrect. 
- "assume that each node is independent of the other" --> In graph learning, this assumption seems to be too strong. 
- Minors:   
> In Eq. (3) and Eq. (4), $z, h$ is common; better change to a more common formation like $<z, h>$.   
> In table 1, 55.2$\pm$2.5 is not the highest performance. If you consider the overlapping confidence interval, bold should be denoted.   
> For the proposed method, -I and -T are indicated; better to also indicate this for the baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The overall organization and writing of this paper are OK and easy to follow.   

The novelty and originality of this work are limited because of the re-use of various successful contrastive learning techniques. The proposed measurement is a minor contribution, but the assumption seems to be too strong, and no further explanation is provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper investigates the effectiveness of graph contrastive learning in the GFL setting by utilizing various successful contrastive / graph contrastive designs. A new measurement is proposed. The performance of the proposed method beats various baselines.   

Overall, the technical contribution and insights from this paper are not sufficient, despite the expected good performance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Contrastive Graph Few-shot Learning framework, which leverages a self-distilled contrastive learning procedure to boost Graph few-shot learning. The proposed model pre-trains a graph encoder with contrastive learning using unlabeled data. Later, the trained encoder is frozen as a teacher model to distill a student model with a contrastive loss. The distilled model is finally fed to few-shot learning. The model learns data representation in a self-supervised manner, thus mitigating the distribution shift impact for better generalization and making model task and data-independent for a general graph mining purpose.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1.	The mechanism of graph few-shot learning is of great importance and applicable to real-world scenarios.
2.	Expensive experiments are conducted in different settings. 

Weaknesses
1.	A major concern is the limited novelty. It seems that the key contribution of the paper is the pre-trained mechanism applied to the task of few-shot graph learning. While the main idea seems plausible, it is not exciting and feels a bit complicated.
2.	The theoretical explanation of the success of the proposed approach should be discussed.
3.	Some experiments are not convictive enough. Concretely, more latest baselines should be considered for comparison.
Recommendation

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper investigates graph few-shot learning. The proposed framework is in 3 stages:

1. Contrastive pretraining (using [BYOL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07733)).
2. Self-distillation pretraining (using [BAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.04770)).
3. Graph few-shot learning (using [ProtoNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.05175)).

The paper also propose to compute the information of the input graph encoded by the GNN hidden state as away to measure model capability. Experiments on few-shot node and graph classification show improvement over baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strength
  - The paper is well written and describes the proposed method well.
  - Experiments show effectiveness of the proposed method over some baselines, though it is required to provide statistical significance or otherwise the performance gap looks rather marginal.

* Weakness
  - The proposed framework is built on a series of well-established methods. Inherently, this makes the presented work incremental. Are there any technical challenges in applying existing methods (BYOL, BAN, ProtoNet) to this problem? What is the technical novelty of this work?
  - It seems there are several works on self-supervised learning of graph neural networks (e.g., [Self-supervised learning of GNN: A unified review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.10757.pdf)). Given that, the selection of BYOL for contrastive pretraining looks somewhat arbitrary and it would be great if authors can comment on its selection over several different options.
  - Are baseline methods evaluated under inductive or transductive settings? If baselines are inductive, the improvement over SOTA seems fairly marginal, given how large their standard deviations are. It would be great if authors can provide statistical significance of the proposed method over some of the baseline methods.
  - The significance and the implication of Section 4.3 Quantitative measurement of GFL are unclear. In experiments, authors claim that smaller info. loss may refer to the better node / graph embeddings. Are there more conclusive evidences (e.g., correlation between the info loss and downstream accuracy)? Would graph autoencoder-like approach result in better info loss already?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The paper is written clearly and well organized. It is easy to read and understand.

* The novelty is limited. The proposed framework employs well established methods without much modification. The paper introduces a new component on measuring information loss, but the significance of the component is not well demonstrated.

* The paper has sufficient information on the parameter settings, etc. Authors provided the code in the supplementary material. Given the complexity of the proposed framework, it would be great if authors can release the source code upon acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a framework for graph few-shot learning by leveraging self-supervised pretraining. While authors demonstrated improvement over baselines, the proposed framework is rather incremental, lack of comparison to other self-supervised graph learning methods baselines, and the improvement over existing works do not look statistically significant given the high variance.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses graph few-shot learning for node classification and graph classification.  The authors propose a Contrastive Graph Few-Shot Learning (GFSL) framework to mitigate distribution shift in the test scenario.  GFSL is composed of two phases: (1) a self-distilled GNN contrastive pre-training phase that learns a distilled GNN using graph augmentations (node feature masking, edge removal, node dropping), and (2) a GNN few-shot learning phase that takes the pretrained GNN and applies meta-learning with few-shot examples.  The authors also presents an information-based method to measure the quality of learned node/graph embeddings.  Experiments were performed on standard graph datasets for both the node classification and graph classification tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
+ The paper is in general well-written and easy to read.
+ The proposed information-based measure for graph embeddings looks sound.

**Weaknesses** (see more details in Feedback)
- The need of two-phase distillation for few-shot adaptation can use stronger rationale and theoretical efforts.
- Experiments seem to miss critical comparisons to SoTA methods.  Data stats also mismatch the reported numbers from previous arts.
- Missing details in experimental setup.

**Feedback**
1. The claim throughout the paper, "learning data representation in a self-supervised manner, thus mitigating the distribution shift impact for better generalization" (eg, in Abstract, last paragraph of Intro), reads generic and should be elaborated.  Please enrich descriptions about which design of self-supervised learning improves generalizability to unseen glasses, and why.

2. Sec 3, Problems 1-2:  Since these problems explicitly state few-shot classification, it is clearer to include in the problem statements the relationship between C_{base} vs C_{novel}, eg, they should be non-overlapping classes, and C_{novel} can have partially labelled or completely unlabelled data for inductive vs transductive settings (ie, CGFL-I vs CGFL-T in Sec 5.1).

3. Provide stronger rationale for the proposed two-phase distillation method.

    a. It is unclear to me why two-phase distillation is needed.  If we have a target GNN already, why not just adopt it for few-shot generalization?  Since both GNNs have the same architecture (mentioned above Eq 3), I do not see immediate benefits of the use of distillation that usually helps reduce unnecessary / redundant information to a more compact model.  In addition, if there is a way to pre-train the target GNN, it should be possible to directly train an "online GNN" with the same data/annotation and the proposed augmentations.  This again renders the distillation seemingly unnecessary.  Please clarify.

    b.  Sec 4.1, above Eq 6: "We load the pretrained GNN f_\theta and take it as the teacher model" further triggers my doubts on the motivation for double distillation (one from target GNN to online GNN, another from online GNN to a student GNN).  Similar to 3.a, it seems possible that the two distillations can be integrated into a joint training step, ie, using target GNN's training data/annotations to distill a model with graph augmentations.  Please elaborate and clarify on the design choice.

    c. Sec 4.2: In the context of few-shot learning, it is relevant (and critical) to describe the choice of the support set.  Please enrich the details about how the support set is defined and its behavior in the inner loop.

4. Please add technical details regarding (a) how unlabeled data is used in training vs test phases, and (b) how the final inference is done (eg, L2 distance or cosine similarity based on the learned normalized embedding?).

5. Experiments

    a. Data stats of Reddit-12K in Table 6 (Appendix A) mismatches the numbers reported in the original paper.  The # of graphs is way smaller than 12K.  Is this a typo or experiments are done with different subsets of the data?  Please clarify.

    b. Sec 5.2: Sampling few-shot examples turns out to be rather critical in the final generalization quality and can cause large variance in the performance.  Please provide more details about how the 3/5-shot samples are selected, and how the final numbers are reported (eg, what is the stopping criteria for few-shot learning; how many experiments were used to report the variance; do all experiments use the exactly the same set of few-shot samples, and if not, could you provide an ablation study with controlled samples to report the performance).

    c. RALE (Liu et al, 2021) also reports on Reddit dataset and shows a better performance on 3/5-shot, though the comparisons seem missing on Table 3.  Please add comparisons and analyze their gaps.

    d. Embedding dimension is another critical detail missing in experiments.  Please explicitly mention the choice of embedding dimension and compare it with choices of existing methods.  If possible please also discuss the sensitivity of embedding dimension against accuracy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The proposed two-phase distillation for graph few-shot learning looks new.  However, the motivation and rationale for the design choice remains unclear to me (as mentioned in the above feedback), pushing the clarity / quality / novelty towards the lower rank.  The lack of technical details in current manuscript also make the paper hard to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: Please see the "Strength And Weaknesses" section.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
